analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement and penalties for paying women less than men for equal work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate committee vote or floor action; it died when the Congress ended in January 2007, with all 19 Senate supporters Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened the Equal Pay Act, the 1963 law against paying women less than men for equal work. It would let workers recover compensatory and punitive damages, bring wage-discrimination cases as class actions, bar employers from punishing workers for discussing their pay, and narrow employers' defenses. It also directed the Labor Department and other agencies to collect pay data, train investigators, run negotiation-skills programs for women, and publish wage-discrimination information.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men doing comparable work would gain a much stronger way to sue and recover. Workers generally would gain the right to ask about and share wage information without retaliation, and the Labor Department would get funding and direction to investigate pay discrimination more actively.

how_it_helps.text: Allows courts to award compensatory and punitive damages to workers who were paid less because of their sex, on top of the back pay available under current law [S3].
Lets wage-discrimination claims proceed as class actions and shifts the burden to employers to prove that a pay gap rests on a genuinely job-related factor other than sex [S3].
Makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against a worker for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages [S3].
Directs the Labor Department to investigate federal contractors' compensation practices more aggressively and to make wage-discrimination information readily available to the public [S2] [S3].
Authorizes grants for negotiation-skills training for girls and women and requires federal agencies to train investigators on wage-discrimination matters [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face higher damages exposure, broader class-action suits, tougher government investigations of federal contractors, and new pay-data reporting. Taxpayers would fund the grant, training, and research programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows the employer's defense and can require employers to prove that pay differences are job-related and reasonably applied, which businesses argued would expose them to costly litigation over pay structures even without intentional discrimination [S3].
Opening wage-discrimination cases to class actions plus compensatory and punitive damages would significantly raise employers' financial risk under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S3].
It authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' without specifying program funding, leaving the cost to appropriations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would flow to workers denied equal pay, a group with little power to negotiate individually, and its enforcement tools address a real gap in the 1963 law's weak remedies. The costs fall on employers through litigation exposure and reporting, which opponents considered substantial but which is the ordinary price of enforcing antidiscrimination law. The design is broadly similar to later versions of the bill that repeatedly failed to pass.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Hillary Clinton introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act in the Senate on April 19, 2005, joined by 18 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced; no further action was taken [S5].
The bill received no committee mark-up, no floor vote, and no House companion action in the record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided the higher damages exposure, class-action risk, and tougher federal contractor investigations it would have created. Women seeking stronger equal-pay remedies gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoided new damages and enforcement risk

for.name: Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton
for.role: Lead sponsor, Senator from New York
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (Republican majority in the 109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the referred bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed versions of the Paycheck Fairness Act as costly litigation exposure for employers

sides.party_line_note: All 19 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the Republican-controlled committee and Senate took no action [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill raises damages exposure, permits class actions over pay discrimination, restricts retaliation against workers who discuss wages, and narrows the defenses employers can use. Its cost falls on businesses; its benefit is enforceable equal pay for workers.

The bill directs the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to use a broader range of investigative tools and to survey half of nonconstruction contractor establishments each year, increasing scrutiny of contractor pay practices.

industries.industry: Temporary and contract staffing firms and other users of pay-secrecy policies
industries.note: The nonretaliation provision would end pay-secrecy practices that make it harder for workers to discover wage differences, an outcome workers gain from and such employers lose.
